blocks.text: On bare metal, each application got its own physical server to avoid conflicts, so hardware sat mostly idle, capacity arrived in weeks, and every server was a unique, hand-maintained machine.

rows: One app per box for isolation; sized for peak
Utilization commonly cited in the ~5-15% range; paying for idle CPU, power, rack space
Procure → rack → cable → install OS → configure
Weeks to months per new environment
Apps share one OS, libraries, ports, users
One app's upgrade or crash affects the others
App tied to a physical host
Failures and migrations mean manual rebuilds

blocks.text: Every later technology answers one of these pains:

items: VMs → utilization and isolation on shared hardware.
Containers → fast, dense, reproducible application packaging.

blocks.text: Running several apps on one server was possible but risky: shared system libraries, port collisions, and a single OS upgrade touching everything. "One app per box" was the defensive default.

Q: "What problem did virtualization and containers originally solve?" A: "Bare-metal servers ran one app each for isolation, leaving most hardware idle and making new environments take weeks. Virtualization consolidated workloads safely onto shared hardware; containers went further, making application packaging lightweight, reproducible and fast to start."

items: One app per server = isolation bought with idle hardware.
Apps sharing one OS share its failure modes.
Each later technology targets one of these pains.
